data.title: Cursor
data.tagline: The mouse pointer changes shape to preview whether an area can be clicked, typed in, dragged, or is currently unavailable
data.description: When a mouse moves over an element, CSS cursor can show a familiar system pointer: pointer for clickable areas, text for editable text, grab for draggable objects, and not-allowed as an extra unavailable-state cue. These shapes vary by platform and cannot replace clear controls, labels, focus styles, or disabled behavior. Touchscreens usually show no mouse pointer. The blinking insertion line inside a text field is the caret, not the mouse pointer.

scenarios: The pointer changes with the drag state
An unavailable action still needs an explanation

lessonPractice.title: A draggable card, text field, and disabled button all show the same hand cursor. How should this be corrected?

options.label: Use grab, text, and not-allowed by actual role while keeping clear control styling
options.feedback: Role-matched cursors preview behavior, while the controls themselves still communicate drag, input, and disabled state.

options.label: Keep pointer everywhere so users know all three regions deserve attention
options.feedback: Pointer usually implies clicking and cannot distinguish dragging, text input, and unavailable actions.

options.label: Remove visual differences between controls and rely only on cursor shape for meaning
options.feedback: Touch has no cursor change, and a cursor is only a secondary cue rather than a visible role or state.

data.agentPrompt: Audit cursor usage: follow the product convention for clickable controls, use text for input, grab and grabbing for drag handles, and not-allowed for disabled actions. Treat cursors as secondary cues and preserve meaning on touch.
